issues.legal_issue: An appeal admitted by certificate is before the court in its full scope, although the court retains discretion to restrict the points argued.
material_facts: The appeal was admitted on a certificate of fitness that identified only one ground.
The respondent objected to the appellant raising points beyond the ground identified in the certificate.
issues.conclusion: The certificate did not by itself prevent the appellant from raising other points; the court could permit them, but retained discretion to refuse a new point.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 133 of the Constitution, once a certificate of fitness is granted, the appeal is before the Supreme Court in its full amplitude. The court may permit any point to be urged, but may use its discretion to disallow a new point. The court relied on the rulings reported at 1963 (2) SCR 440 and 1964 (2) SCR 930.

predicates.appeal_admitted_by_certificate: The case is an appeal admitted to the court by a certificate of fitness.
predicates.additional_point_proposed: The appellant seeks to argue a point beyond the ground identified in the certificate.
predicates.court_may_permit_additional_point: The court may allow the appellant to argue the additional point.

issues.definition: When an appeal is admitted by certificate and an appellant proposes an additional point, the court may allow that point to be argued.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord seeking eviction under rent-control law must establish a right to possession under the general law as well as a ground for eviction under the rent-control law.
material_facts: The landlord proved grounds for eviction under rent-control law, including unauthorized subletting and the tenant’s acquisition of alternative accommodation.
The tenancy had not been terminated by a notice to quit.
The court treated the rent-control law as supplementing, rather than replacing, the requirements governing termination of the tenancy under the general law.
issues.conclusion: A landlord cannot obtain an eviction order merely by proving a rent-control ground; the landlord must also establish a valid determination of the tenancy under the general law.
issues.legal_principle: Rent-control statutes ordinarily protect tenants by adding restrictions on eviction rather than creating a new right of action for landlords. Unless a statute expressly supersedes the general law, a landlord must establish both a right to possession under the general law and a statutory ground for eviction. The court relied on Manujendra Dutt, Abasbhai v. Gulamnabi, and Mangilal v. Sugan Chand.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The landlord seeks possession through an eviction proceeding governed by rent-control law.
predicates.rent_control_ground_proved: The landlord proves a ground for eviction specified by the applicable rent-control law.
predicates.tenancy_not_validly_determined: The landlord has not established that the tenancy was validly determined under the applicable general law.
predicates.eviction_order_unavailable: The landlord cannot obtain an eviction order on the rent-control ground alone.

issues.definition: In a rent-control eviction proceeding, proof of a statutory ground does not permit an eviction order if the tenancy has not also been validly determined.

issues.legal_issue: A lease stated only to be for a period of less than one year is for an indefinite period and does not expire merely by efflux of time.
material_facts: The lease described its term only as a period of less than one year.
The landlord argued that the lease had expired by efflux of time, but the court rejected that argument.
issues.conclusion: The lease was for an indefinite period and could not be treated as having expired by efflux of time.
issues.legal_principle: A lease that merely states that it is for a period of less than one year does not specify a definite term and is therefore for an indefinite period; it cannot expire by efflux of time on that wording alone.

predicates.lease_term_stated_only_as_less_than_one_: The lease describes its duration only as a period of less than one year and states no definite end date or term.
predicates.lease_does_not_expire_by_efflux_of_time: The lease does not end merely through the passage of the stated period.

issues.definition: If a lease states only that its term is less than one year, it does not expire merely by efflux of time.

issues.legal_issue: Where the governing principles of justice, equity and good conscience apply, filing an eviction proceeding can determine a lease by forfeiture without a formal written notice if the lessee breached a condition providing for re-entry and the lessor thereby communicated an election to eject.
material_facts: The lease was made before the relevant statutory regime was extended to the area, and the appellant had relied below on justice, equity and good conscience rather than on the statute applying of its own force.
The lease contained a condition against subletting and provided for the landlord to seek eviction upon breach.
The tenant sublet part of the premises in breach of that condition.
The landlord filed an eviction proceeding, but gave no separate written notice of forfeiture.
The court held that the filing of the proceeding communicated the landlord’s election to eject and that a formal written notice was not a requirement of justice, equity and good conscience.
issues.conclusion: The lease was validly determined by forfeiture when the landlord instituted the eviction proceeding; a separate written notice of forfeiture was unnecessary.
issues.legal_principle: The essential equitable requirements for forfeiture are breach of a lease condition providing for re-entry and an overt act by the lessor communicating an election to determine the lease on that breach. The written-notice formality in section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act is statutory and technical, not an essential rule of justice, equity and good conscience. The court relied on Namdeo Lokman Lodhi v. Narmada Bai, distinguished Mohd. Amir, and treated the pre-amendment principle reflected in section 111(g) as consistent with justice, equity and good conscience. It also rejected the notion that English law should be followed as such.

rule.if: forfeiture_ejectment_proceeding and lease_condition_provides_for_reentry and lessee_breached_condition and lessor_filed_ejectment

predicates.forfeiture_ejectment_proceeding: The case concerns an eviction proceeding in which the lessor seeks to eject the lessee for breach of a lease condition.
predicates.lease_condition_provides_for_reentry: The lease provides for the lessor to recover possession or seek eviction if the specified condition is breached.
predicates.lessee_breached_condition: The lessee breached the condition that provides for the lessor to seek recovery of possession.
predicates.lessor_filed_ejectment: The lessor filed a proceeding seeking to eject the lessee on the basis of the breach.
predicates.lease_determined_by_filing_ejectment: The filing of the ejectment proceeding determines the lease by communicating the lessor’s election to eject for the breach.

issues.definition: In a forfeiture-based ejectment proceeding, when the lease provides for recovery of possession on breach, the lessee breaches that condition, and the lessor files to eject, the filing communicates the lessor’s election and determines the lease.

issues.legal_issue: A court may refuse to permit an appellant to advance a new statutory basis that was not pursued below and conflicts with the basis on which the appellant consistently relied.
material_facts: The appellant had relied in the lower courts and in the grounds of appeal on principles of justice, equity and good conscience rather than on the statutory provisions applying of their own force.
The appellant advanced the new statutory contention for the first time in the Supreme Court.
The court had discretion to permit a new point but declined to exercise it in these circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The court refused to permit the appellant to shift to the new statutory contention and decided the matter on the basis the appellant had previously maintained.
issues.legal_principle: Although an appeal admitted by certificate is before the court in its full scope, the court retains discretion to refuse a new point. The court applied that discretion because the appellant had not advanced the statutory theory below and had consistently relied on a different legal basis.

predicates.certificate_appeal: The case is an appeal admitted by certificate.
predicates.new_statutory_point_not_raised_below: The appellant did not advance the statutory argument in the courts below.
predicates.appellant_consistently_relied_on_differe: The appellant consistently relied on a different legal basis in the courts below and in the appeal grounds.
predicates.court_may_refuse_new_point: The court may decline to allow the appellant to advance the new point.

issues.definition: In a certificate appeal, if an appellant raises a statutory point for the first time after consistently relying on a different basis, the court may refuse to hear that new point.
